title: Designing Google Docs

facts.text: The system must merge edits from different users on different devices automatically and almost instantly. Real-time groupware needs fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times.
The groupware concurrency algorithm of Ellis and colleagues is simple and responsive: users operate directly on the data without obtaining locks.
Clients send document editing operations to the WebSocket server, which handles the real-time communication.
Document operations are persisted in a message queue, and the file operation server consumes them and generates transformed operations using collaboration algorithms.
Three types of data are stored: file metadata, file content and operations.

One of the biggest challenges is real-time conflict resolution. Users need their own edits shown instantly, but because of network latency those edits are applied to different versions of the document.
If Bob turns Mary into Hary while Alice turns it into My, each receives edits made against versions that never existed locally, so remote edits must be applied despite conflicts with local ones.
Common conflict-resolution algorithms are operational transformation (OT), differential synchronization (DS) and conflict-free replicated data types (CRDT).
With OT each client holds its own replica, edits it without locks, and transforms changes received from others before executing them, which suits high-latency environments such as the web.

OT adjusts an operation's parameters for concurrent operations already executed. After inserting x at position 0 of abc, deleting position 2 must become position 3; untransformed, it deletes b instead of c.
OT must keep causality (operations execute in their cause-effect order) and convergence (all copies identical once every operation has run), and intention preservation is a further goal.
OT is hard to get right: formal proofs are complicated and error-prone, a former Google Wave engineer found implementing it painful, and every change to the data must be captured.
A sequence CRDT can build a collaborative real-time editor as an alternative to OT; differential synchronization is another alternative.
The guide says Google Docs uses OT per its Wikipedia page, and OT was adopted in 2009 as a core technique behind Google Wave and Google Docs; CRDT remains an active research area.

A basic alternative is a client-server model where one editor acts as the collaboration server; changes may not show on a client until the server answers. It is less powerful but cheap, suiting limited processing resources.

notes: thin: the sources give no scale or estimates, document data model detail, API, permissions, version history or offline editing, and no explanation of how differential synchronization works (no page crawled).

definition.text: A technique for keeping replicated documents consistent under concurrent edits by transforming each operation's parameters against the effects of concurrent operations already executed.

facts.text: OT was invented for consistency maintenance and concurrency control in collaborative editing of plain text, and was pioneered in 1989 by Ellis and Gibbs. It was adopted in 2009 as a core technique behind Google Wave and Google Docs.

Each client holds its own copy and edits it without locking or blocking; changes are propagated and each receiver transforms them before executing, so all sites keep their consistency invariants and the client stays responsive despite latency.
With the text abc, O1 = insert x at 0 and O2 = delete c at 2: after O1, O2 must become delete at 3. Untransformed, it would delete b instead of c.

Collaborative editing needs causality preservation (operations run in cause-effect order) and convergence (all copies identical once all operations have run); the CCI model adds intention preservation.

An OT system separates the high-level control algorithm, which decides which operations are transformed against which, from the low-level transformation functions, which transform a pair of operations by type and position.
The first OT system used a single linear address space with character-wise insert and delete; the model was later extended with an update operation and hierarchies of addressing domains.

Property TP1 requires that applying op1 then the transformed op2 equals applying op2 then the transformed op1 for concurrent operations on the same state; TP2 extends this to three concurrent operations.

OT is hard to get right: formal proofs are complicated and error-prone, implementing it is painful per a former Google Wave engineer, and every edit must be captured. Differential synchronization and sequence CRDTs are alternatives.

definition.text: Letting several users edit the same document at once on different devices, with their edits merged automatically and nearly instantly.

facts.text: Real-time editing synchronizes the edits of all online users automatically and periodically, often nearly instantly, which avoids or minimizes edit conflicts.
Asynchronous editing (delayed or offline) makes each user submit, update and merge manually, so several users can edit the same line and cause conflicts needing manual merging or overwriting.
The difficulty is communication latency. Users need their own edits incorporated instantly, yet instant incorporation means edits land in different versions of the document.
If Bob turns Mary into Hary while Alice turns it into My, each receives edits made on versions that never existed locally; the task is applying such remote edits that may conflict with local ones.
The most sophisticated solutions need no server, use no locking, so all users edit all parts at once, and support any number of users, limited only by their computers.

A basic client-server design makes one editor the collaboration server, which receives timestamped change notifications and broadcasts its changes; it is less powerful but cheap, suiting limited processing resources.
Workspace approaches that lock the document or reconcile conflicting changes are generally found unsatisfactory by users.
A sequence CRDT can serve as an alternative to operational transformation; Microsoft's Fluid Framework instead relies on total order broadcast, as opposed to OT or CRDT.

title: Groupware concurrency control

definition.text: Concurrency control for groupware, computer systems that support two or more users working on a common task through a shared environment.

facts.text: Groupware systems often require fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times. The paper separates real-time groupware from other multi-user systems and sets out their concurrency control requirements.
It presents a concurrency control algorithm for real-time groupware whose advantages are simplicity of use and responsiveness: users operate directly on the data without obtaining locks.
The algorithm must know some semantics of the operations, but its overall structure is independent of that information, so it can be adapted to many situations.
It is applied to group text editing, with a proof sketch, and the paper notes that the behavior wanted in many such systems is non-serializable.

notes: The 1989 paper by Ellis and Gibbs that introduced the approach later called operational transformation; abstract only.
